column1: # Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam — Hadith 44: “Nursing makes unlawful what birth makes unlawful”

column2: From ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “Nursing makes unlawful what birth makes unlawful.” Al-Bukhārī and Muslim recorded it.
The two of them recorded this hadith in the two Ṣaḥīḥs through the narration of ʿAmrah, from ʿĀʾishah. Muslim also recorded, through the narration of ʿUrwah, from ʿĀʾishah, that the Prophet ﷺ said:

“What is unlawful through lineage is unlawful through nursing.” They also recorded it through the narration of ʿUrwah from ʿĀʾishah as her own words, and recorded it from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ;
and al-Tirmidhī recorded it from the hadith of ʿAlī, from the Prophet ﷺ.

The scholars are agreed on acting on these hadiths in general, and on the principle that nursing makes unlawful what lineage makes unlawful. Let us mention all the women made unlawful by lineage, so that what nursing makes unlawful may be known from it. We say: birth and lineage may make marriage unlawful, and this is of two categories.
The first is permanent unlawfulness of marrying a woman on her own, and it is of two kinds.
The first kind is what is unlawful by lineage alone. Unlawful to a man are his ascendants, however high; his descendants, however low; the descendants of his nearest ascendants, however low;

and the immediate offspring of his more distant ascendants, but not their offspring. Included in his ascendants are his mothers, however high, on his father's side and his mother's; in his descendants, his daughters and his children's daughters, however low;

in the descendants of his nearest ascendants, his sisters, whether full or through one parent, their daughters, and the daughters of his brothers and of their children, however low; and in the offspring of his more distant ascendants, his paternal and maternal aunts and the paternal and maternal aunts of his parents, however high.

So of his female relatives none remain lawful to a man but the further descendants of his more distant ascendants, namely the daughters of his paternal uncles and paternal aunts and the daughters of his maternal uncles and maternal aunts.
The second kind is what is unlawful by lineage together with another cause, namely relationship by marriage (muṣāharah).
Unlawful to a man are the wives of his fathers, the wives of his sons, the mothers of his wives, and the daughters of those wives with whom he has consummated marriage.

Thus unlawful to a man are his wife's mother and her mothers on the mother's and the father's side, however high; unlawful to him are his wife's daughters — the stepdaughters (rabāʾib) — and their daughters, however low; and likewise the daughters of his wife's sons, who count as the daughters of the stepchildren. Al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad stated this explicitly, and no disagreement on it is known.
It is unlawful for him to marry his father's wife, however high the father, or his son's wife, however low the son. That these come under unlawfulness by lineage is evident,
since their unlawfulness arises from the man's own lineage together with the cause of marriage relationship.

As for the mothers of his wives and their daughters, their unlawfulness, together with marriage relationship, is due to the woman's lineage, so in their case too the unlawfulness does not cease to be by lineage joined to the cause of marriage relationship. Unlawfulness by lineage alone, and by lineage added to marriage relationship, applies to men and women alike.

It is unlawful for a woman to marry her ascendants, however high; her descendants, however low; the descendants of her nearest ascendants, however low — her brothers and her brothers' children, however low; and the offspring of her more distant ascendants — the paternal and maternal uncles, however high — but not their sons. All this is by lineage alone.

As for lineage added to marriage relationship: it is unlawful for her to marry her husband's father, however high, and his son, however low, by the mere contract; and unlawful to her are her daughter's husband, however low the daughter, by the contract, and her mother's husband, however high the mother, but on condition that he has consummated marriage with the mother.

The second category is permanent unlawfulness of combining two women, not of marrying either one alone. This unlawfulness is specific to men, since a woman can never be permitted to have two husbands at once.
Any two women between whom there is a prohibiting tie of kinship — such that, if one of them were male, he could not marry the other — may not be combined in marriage.
Al-Shaʿbī said: The Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ used to say: A man may not combine two women such that, if one of them were a man, it would not be right for him to marry her.

This is when the unlawfulness arises from lineage, and that is how Sufyān al-Thawrī and most scholars explained it. If it arises from something other than lineage — for example, combining a man's wife and his daughter by another woman — that is permissible according to most scholars, though some of the Salaf disliked it.
Once what lineage makes unlawful is known, then for everything it makes unlawful, its counterpart through nursing is unlawful too. It is unlawful for a man to marry his foster mothers, however high,
his foster daughters, however low, his foster sisters, the daughters of his foster sisters, and his foster paternal and maternal aunts, however high, but not their daughters.
This means that when a woman nurses a child with a nursing that counts, within the period that counts, she becomes his mother by the text of the Book of Allah,
so she and her mothers, however high, whether by lineage or by nursing, become unlawful to him; and all her daughters become his foster sisters, and so are unlawful to him by the text of the Qurʾān.

The rest of what nursing makes unlawful was learned from the Sunnah, just as it was learned from the Sunnah that the unlawfulness of combining is not confined to two sisters, but applies equally to a woman and her paternal aunt and to a woman and her maternal aunt. Since the children of the nursing woman, by lineage or by nursing, are siblings of the nursed child,

the daughters of his siblings are also unlawful to him. The Prophet ﷺ declined to marry the daughter of Ḥamzah and the daughter of Abū Salamah, giving as his reason that their fathers were his foster brothers.
Also unlawful to him are the sisters of the nursing woman,

since they are his maternal aunts. The unlawfulness also extends to the man (faḥl) whose milk it is, from whom the child was nursed: he becomes the child's father, and all his children, whether by the nursing woman

or by another, by lineage or by nursing, become siblings of the nursed child, and his brothers become the nursed child's paternal uncles. This is the view of the majority of scholars among the Salaf, and the four imams and those after them were agreed on it.

This is shown from the Sunnah by what ʿĀʾishah narrated: Aflaḥ, the brother of Abū al-Quʿays, asked permission to come in to see her after the verse of the veil had been revealed. ʿĀʾishah said: I said:

By Allah, I will not give him permission until I have asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, for it was not Abū al-Quʿays who nursed me; it was his wife who nursed me. She said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came in, I mentioned that to him, and he said: “Give him permission,
for he is your uncle — may your right hand be covered in dust!” Abū al-Quʿays was the husband of the woman who had nursed ʿĀʾishah.
The two of them recorded it in the two Ṣaḥīḥs with this meaning.
Ibn ʿAbbās was asked about a man who had two slave women, one of whom nursed a girl and the other a boy: may the boy marry the girl? He said: No; the milk comes from one and the same man.
If the milk by which the child was nursed came to the woman without intercourse with a man — for example, a woman with no husband who has come to have milk, or one who is a virgin or past menopause —

most scholars hold that nursing with it creates unlawfulness, and the nursing woman becomes the child's mother. Ibn al-Mundhir related this as the consensus of those people of knowledge whose views are recorded; it is the view of Abū Ḥanīfah, Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Isḥāq and others.
Imam Aḥmad, in the well-known position explicitly reported from him, held that it creates no unlawfulness at all unless there is a man through whom the milk flows.
A view like this has been related from al-Shāfiʿī.
If the child's lineage from the man whose milk it is has been cut off — as with a child born of fornication — does the unlawfulness extend to the fornicator whose milk it is?
This rests on whether a daughter born of fornication is unlawful to the fornicator.

The school of Abū Ḥanīfah and Aḥmad, and of Mālik in one reported position, is that she is unlawful to him, contrary to al-Shāfiʿī; and Imam Aḥmad was very severe in condemning those who disagreed on this. On their view, does the unlawfulness extend to the fornicator whose milk it is, so that he becomes the father of the nursed child, or not?
There are two views on this, which are two views within our school. Ibn Ḥāmid chose that the unlawfulness does not extend to him, while Abū Bakr

and al-Qāḍī Abū Yaʿlā chose that it does extend to the fornicator. This is Aḥmad's explicit statement, which he related from Ibn ʿAbbās; and it is the view of Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh, which Ḥarb transmitted from him.

Unlawfulness through nursing extends to what is unlawful through lineage together with marriage relationship — whether through the man's lineage, such as his father's wife and his son's wife, or through the wife's lineage, such as her mother and her daughter — and also to the combining that is unlawful because of the women's lineage,

such as combining two sisters, or a woman and her paternal or maternal aunt. All of this is unlawful through nursing as it is through lineage, since it falls under his words ﷺ: “What is unlawful through lineage is unlawful through nursing.”

All of this is unlawful because of lineage — some of it because of the husband's lineage and some because of the wife's. The imams of the Salaf stated this explicitly, and no disagreement among them on it is known. Imam Aḥmad stated it explicitly, arguing from the general sense of his words:
“What is unlawful through lineage is unlawful through nursing.”

As for His words, Mighty and Majestic is He, “and the wives of your sons who are from your own loins” [al-Nisāʾ 4:23], they said: He did not mean by this that the wives of foster sons are not unlawful; He meant only to exclude the wives of those who had been adopted as sons
without being sons by lineage, as the Prophet ﷺ married the wife of Zayd ibn Ḥārithah after having adopted him.
This unlawfulness through nursing is specific to the nursed child himself and extends to his children. It does not extend to those on the nursed child's level, his brothers and sisters,

nor to those above him, his fathers, mothers, paternal uncles and aunts and maternal uncles and aunts. So the nursing woman herself is lawful to the nursed child's father by lineage and to his brother by lineage; and the nursed child's mother by lineage, and his sister by lineage, are lawful to his foster father and to his foster brother.

This is the view of the majority of scholars. They said: A man may marry the sister of his foster brother, and the sister of his foster daughter — so much so that al-Shaʿbī said: She is more lawful than the water of Qadas. Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit and Aḥmad stated explicitly that she is lawful.

Ashʿath narrated from al-Ḥasan that he disliked a man's marrying the daughter of his son's wet nurse, saying: She is his son's sister; yet he saw no harm in his marrying her mother, meaning his son's wet nurse. Sulaymān al-Taymī narrated from al-Ḥasan

that he was asked about a man marrying the sister of his foster brother and said nothing on it, which implies that he withheld judgement. Perhaps al-Ḥasan disliked it only as something mildly disapproved, not as unlawful, because it resembles in name what is unlawful by lineage; and that alone does not make anything unlawful.
Many jurists of our school and others have excepted two cases from among those unlawful by lineage, saying that their counterparts through nursing are not unlawful.
The first is the sister's mother: she is unlawful by lineage but not through nursing.
The second is the son's sister: she is unlawful by lineage but not through nursing. But there is no need to except these two, or either of them.
As for the sister's mother, she is unlawful by lineage only because she is one's mother or one's father's wife, not merely because she is a sister's mother;

and unlawfulness is not to be attached to what Allah has not attached it to. Through nursing, then, there may be a woman who is a sister's mother without being one's mother or one's father's wife, and she is not unlawful,

because she is not the counterpart of the woman related by lineage. As for the son's sister, Allah the Exalted made unlawful only the stepdaughter whose mother one has consummated marriage with: she is unlawful because she is such a stepdaughter, not because she is one's son's sister. In nursing there is no consummation, so the children of the nursing woman are not made unlawful by it.

Among what may fall under the general sense of his words, “What is unlawful through lineage is unlawful through nursing,” is this: if a man makes ẓihār against his wife — likening her to a woman forbidden to him — and likens her to a woman unlawful to him through nursing, saying, “You are to me like my foster mother,” is the unlawfulness of ẓihār established by that or not? There are two views:

The first is that the unlawfulness of ẓihār is established by it. This is the view of the majority, among them Mālik, al-Thawrī, Abū Ḥanīfah, al-Awzāʿī, al-Ḥasan ibn Ṣāliḥ and ʿUthmān al-Battī, and it is the well-known position of Aḥmad.
The second is that the unlawfulness is not established by it. This is the view of al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad withheld judgement on it in the narration of Ibn Manṣūr.
